query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 2–3 atomic percent aluminum to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in-situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature exposure in air, thereby significantly improving its oxygen resistance while preserving its room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (~2–3 at%) aluminum addition into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature air exposure at temperatures between 800 °C and 1000 °C for an exposure period of 5 hours under strain rates ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 oxide scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum has a high affinity for oxygen and forms a dense, protective Al2O3 scale when exposed to high temperatures. This scale impedes further oxygen diffusion into the alloy, thereby mitigating oxidation (pesting) without significantly altering the bulk microstructure responsible for the alloy’s favorable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in oxygen ingress (as evidenced by lower oxygen weight gain and intact scale adherence) compared to the untreated material, while retaining its as-cast high ductility and yield strength characteristics during high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The untreated, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which under similar conditions undergoes rapid oxidation and pesting, leading to compromised surface integrity.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for high-temperature applications in air at 800–1000 °C for exposure durations of approximately 5 hours under the specified mechanical strain-rate conditions. Its validity beyond these conditions is not established.
generation.uncertainty: There is residual uncertainty regarding whether the low aluminum content might inadvertently promote the formation of unwanted secondary phases or alter the as-cast microstructure sufficiently to affect room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast alloy samples: one set with the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition and a second set with the same composition modified by the addition of 2–3 at% aluminum. Subject both sets to identical testing conditions: exposure in air at 800–1000 °C for 5 hours, under tensile loading (strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹). Assess the formation, continuity, and adhesion of surface oxides, and subsequently measure oxygen weight gain and mechanical properties (room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength).
measurements: Surface oxide scale thickness and adherence (via microscopy and adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake (or fails to form a continuous, protective Al2O3 scale) compared to the untreated alloy, or if its room-temperature ductility/high-temperature yield strength is significantly degraded relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

decision.trend: Earlier studies in refractory high‐entropy alloys and related systems have addressed oxidation and mechanical performance issues by making modest compositional modifications to trigger in‐situ formation of protective secondary phases. For example, PMC7513042 demonstrated that introducing reactive elements into a NbMoCrTiAl alloy led to the in‐situ formation of ceramic phases (TiC and Al2O3) that acted to mitigate high‐temperature degradation, while PMC10759803 showed that a small compositional change (adding Cr) in a Hf-containing alloy influenced the phase balance and mechanical performance. In related, non‐equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloys, an oxidation‐protection intervention successfully prevented “pesting” during 5‐hour air exposures at 800 °C. However, none of these studies have directly established a strategy for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr. The trend has therefore been to explore slight compositional shifts that promote the nucleation of protective surface (or near-surface) phases without dramatically altering the as‐cast microstructure or compromising room‐ and high‐temperature properties.
decision.unsolved: For the equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, the challenge remains to enhance oxygen resistance (preventing oxidation-driven pesting) during prolonged high-temperature air exposures while preserving the unique combination of room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength. The effective intervention seen in related non-equiatomic alloys has not yet been translated to the equiatomic composition, leaving open the question of how to induce a protective surface scale or in-situ phase without complex processing or significant degradation of the cast-state mechanical performance.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor (~2–3 at%) reactive element—specifically aluminum—into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition to promote the formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure.
decision.why: Aluminum is well known for its ability to form a dense, slow-growing oxide (Al2O3) that drastically reduces oxygen ingress and surface pesting. This lever follows the trend of slight compositional modifications used in other refractory HEAs (as seen in PMC7513042 and the related non-equiatomic oxidation‐protection studies) to achieve protective oxide formation while minimally perturbing the cast microstructure. A controlled experiment would involve comparing the oxygen weight gain, scale adherence, and retention of tensile ductility and yield strength (at conditions such as 800–1000 °C for 5 h in air at strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) between the base and Al-modified alloys. If the Al-added alloy fails to form a stable Al2O3 layer or shows degraded mechanical properties relative to untreated material, the hypothesis would be falsified.
